history.text: Council Bluffs was out of attainment for lead; its monitor exceeded the standard six times in 2010.
EPA fined Griffin Pipe $950,000 over lead emissions; the plant closed in 2014.
Iowa DNR reports no Iowa facility now emits over 0.5 tons of lead a year.
Leaded aviation fuel for piston-engine aircraft is a remaining national source of airborne lead.

detonation_2026.site: Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, Middletown (Des Moines County)
detonation_2026.plan: Two controlled detonations of degraded lead azide set for about 9 a.m. CST, inside earth-covered concrete magazines ringed with sand barriers, with wetted soil and water misters to hold dust down
detonation_2026.lead_azide_note: About 68 barrels, reported as roughly 10,000 pounds or 5 tons

facts.text: It went ahead: about 9,700 lb in 68 barrels, set off as two simultaneous detonations at about 9 a.m. CT. The Army says all of the lead azide was destroyed.

The Army's Nov 24 forecast had winds from the northeast, with fallout across a narrow stretch of southeast Iowa and northeast Missouri, and dust aloft toward Kirksville and US 36 about eight hours later.
The Army's maps put the strongest effects within about 30 square miles of the plant, with the dust cloud able to travel up to 100 miles.
About 350 farms could be in the plume's path, per USDA. Iowa HHS says this is a projection, not confirmed contamination.
The Army says its modeling shows airborne lead may rise but stay well below the level where EPA requires protective action. It published no number.
The Army cited a 1977 Colorado detonation that kept 75% of its lead on site.

EPA and the Army are sampling air, soil and surfaces before, during and after, with soil and wipe sampling within 24 hours where modeled deposition passes a permit threshold. No results were published in the sources read on Nov 25.
EPA says its real-time air monitors showed zero detection of airborne lead about an hour after the blast. It gave no concentrations or detection limits, and no soil, dust or forage results yet.
The Army's modeled ground deposit contours were 5 µg/ft² (light, 0.05 mg/m²) and 100 µg/ft² (heavier, nearer the site, 1.1 mg/m²). These are model runs, not measurements.
About 350 farms across Iowa and Missouri could lie in the projected plume area, per USDA. No agency has named which counties or farms.

guidance.text: Keep windows and doors closed for 24 to 48 hours and set heating or cooling to recirculate.
Protect livestock feed and water from dust. Ask IDALS and USDA about crops, feed and food production.
Bring animals, hay bales and water indoors.
guidance.note: Iowa Department of Agriculture advice before the earlier date

guidance.text: Wet-clean surfaces children touch, like play equipment and windowsills. Don't dry sweep.
Move or tarp hay and feed, ask the Army for soil and forage samples, have a vet watch animals, and keep expense records for claims to the Army.

army_contours_mg_m2.note: 5 and 100 micrograms per square foot converted at 10.764 square feet per square meter

history.text: The plant has been a Superfund site since 1990. EPA found lead in its sludges and in Brush Creek sediment in 1984.
The pollution documented off the plant is explosives (RDX, TNT) in creeks and private wells to the south, not lead on farms.
